## How to Use This Two-Stage Blind Checkpoint

You have just completed **Part III (Chapters 9–13)**:

- **Chapter 9**: Divide-and-Conquer (CDQ) NTT, Semi-Online Systems & Relaxed (Online) Convolution
- **Chapter 10**: Implicit Functional Equations & Polynomial Newton Iteration
- **Chapter 11**: Formal Laurent Series, Residue Calculus, Raney's Lemma & The 6-Form / Characteristic-$p$ Lagrange Inversion Theorem
- **Chapter 12**: Pointed Rooted Trees, Cactus Graphs & Block-Cut Unicyclic/Biconnected Decomposition
- **Chapter 13**: Labeled Graphical EGFs, $2^{\binom{n}{2}}$ Chirp-Z Edge Convolutions, DAGs & Symbolic Matrix-Tree Determinant Calculus

In individual chapter exercises, the surrounding section header tells you whether to set up a semi-online CDQ recurrence, differentiate an implicit tree equation, change variables inside a formal residue, or apply generalized Cayley forest completion. In a real contest, **nobody labels the paradigm**. A problem about circular floral matchings, binary strings with majority intervals, parking sequences, or pairs of spanning trees arrives purely as a raw combinatorial specification and a table of constraints.

This checkpoint is engineered in **two strict stages**:

1. **Stage 1 — The Blind Diagnostic Arena**: Eight contest problems (`CP-III.1` through `CP-III.8`) are presented in randomized order with **zero paradigm labels** and **zero chapter hints**. For each problem, first work through its small hand-checkable trace ($N \le 4$), then classify its structural signals using the **3-Axis Diagnostic Protocol** below. If you get stuck, open the three progressive hints (`Hint 1` is 100% spoiler-free and purely combinatorial; `Hint 2` reveals the diagnostic signal and target chapter; `Hint 3` gives the core algebraic equation).
2. **Stage 2 — The Master Diagnostic Routing Table & Complete Solutions**: Only after you have committed to a paradigm and functional equation for all eight problems should you expand Stage 2 to audit your routing accuracy and study the complete, step-by-step derivations, failure-mode warnings, and algorithm contracts.
:::

## The Part III Blind Diagnostic Protocol

When facing an unlabeled counting or algebraic extraction problem that goes beyond explicit rational/exponential closed forms (Parts I–II), run it through the following **three diagnostic axes** before writing down any generating function:

1. **Axis 1 — Dependency Topology (Explicit vs. Semi-Online DP vs. Self-Referential Implicit Grammar)**:
   - Does the state at size $n$ depend linearly on all previous sizes $0 \le k < n$ via fixed transition weights $P(x)$ (or a small $d \times d$ matrix of coupled boundary states), or via an interval-monotonicity constraint on a given input array?
   - Or is the combinatorial object defined **recursively in terms of itself** through non-linear branching, tree children, excursion nesting, or block inflation ($F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))$ or $H(x, F(x)) = 0$)?
2. **Axis 2 — Extraction Regime & Arithmetic Field ($[x^0 \dots x^N]$ All-Coefficients vs. Single $[x^N]$ vs. Arbitrary / Small Prime $p$)**:
   - Do you need the **entire coefficient array** up to $N \le 10^5$ modulo an NTT prime $998244353$ (pointing to $O(N \log^2 N)$ CDQ divide-and-conquer or $O(N \log N)$ Newton iteration)?
   - Or do you need a **single coefficient** at an extreme index ($N \le 10^9$ or $N \le 10^{18}$), or modulo an **arbitrary prime $p$** (not NTT-friendly) or a **small prime $p \le 10^5 \ll N$** where $p \mid N$ causes division by $N$ and $\exp/\ln$ to crash with division by zero?
3. **Axis 3 — Combinatorial Symmetry & Graph-Theoretic Incidence Structure**:
   - Does the problem exhibit **cyclic shift invariance** on a circle of length $n+1$ (where every shift orbit contains a unique valid prefix walk), or **edge-sharing / vertex-pair** interactions ($2^{\binom{k}{2}}$ edge subsets, spanning forests $S \subseteq E(T_1) \cap E(T_2)$ of connected component sizes $s_1, \dots, s_k$ weighted by $\prod_{i=1}^k s_i$)?

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Start["Unlabeled Combinatorial or Algebraic Problem"] --> Q1{"What is the dependency structure?"}
    Q1 -->|"Linear transition over prefix/interval states"| Q2{"Single sequence or coupled boundary states?"}
    Q2 -->|"Coupled boundary states on a cycle or strip"| A1["Coupled Matrix Recurrence on Prefix Slices"]
    Q2 -->|"Monotone queue/layer intervals with 2^(free edges)"| A2["Layer-Interval DP with Power-of-2 Edge Factors"]
    Q1 -->|"Product of N distinct capped or sparse polynomials"| A3["Log-Sum / Pentagonal Product Grouping"]
    Q1 -->|"Self-referential tree, excursion, or inflation grammar"| Q3{"What are the target query and modulus?"}
    Q3 -->|"All coefficients up to N <= 10^5 mod 998244353"| A4["Implicit Functional Equation & Compositional Inverse"]
    Q3 -->|"Arbitrary prime p, dyadic/excursion walk of length 2n"| A5["Implicit Excursion Parameter & Change of Variables"]
    Q3 -->|"Huge n <= 10^18 and small prime p <= 10^5 (p | n possible)"| A6["Division-Free Extraction & Base-p Digit Decimation"]
    Q1 -->|"Cyclic walk or labeled spanning trees/graphs"| Q4{"What is the symmetry or graph weight?"}
    Q4 -->|"Prefix dominance sum_i (a_j <= i) >= i with k-th power moments"| A7["Circular Shift Orbit Symmetry & Falling-Factorial Moments"]
    Q4 -->|"Pairs of labeled trees weighted by y^(n - |E1 cap E2|)"| A8["Shared-Forest Subset Expansion & Component Weighting"]
```

### Problem `CP-III.1` (`#090`) — Days of Floral Colours

- **Source**: [Codeforces 848E — Days of Floral Colours](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/848/E) (Codeforces Round 431, Div. 1, Problem E)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Around the perimeter of a circular clock there are $2n$ cells numbered $0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$ in clockwise order. You wish to partition the $2n$ cells into $n$ disjoint unordered pairs of identical flowers (two pairs are not distinguished by color label; only the matching of the $2n$ positions matters) subject to the following rules:

1. **Allowed Pair Distances**: For every matched pair $(u, v)$, the circular distance $\min\big((u - v) \bmod 2n,\, (v - u) \bmod 2n\big)$ must belong to $\{1, 2, n\}$. A pair at distance $n$ (directly across the center of the circle) is called an **opposite pair**.
2. **Central Symmetry**: The matching must be centrally symmetric: for every pair $(u, v)$, the diametrically opposite cells $\big((u + n) \bmod 2n,\, (v + n) \bmod 2n\big)$ must also be matched to each other.
3. **Arc Beauty**: There must be **at least one** opposite pair. When all opposite pairs are removed from the circle, the remaining unmatched cells split into $2m$ contiguous arcs along the circle (since opposite pairs come in antipodal pairs $(i_r, i_r + n)$, these $2m$ arcs consist of $m$ antipodal pairs of arcs of equal lengths $L_1, L_1, L_2, L_2, \dots, L_m, L_m$). The **beauty** of the matching is the product of the lengths of all $2m$ arcs:
   $$\text{Beauty} = \prod_{r=1}^{m} L_r^2.$$
   (If two opposite pairs are adjacent along the circle, the arc between them has length $L_r = 0$, so the beauty of that matching is $0$.)

Given $n$, compute the sum of beauties over all valid matchings modulo $998244353$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 5 \times 10^4$, modulus $p = 998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(n \log^2 n)$ (or $O(n)$) time and $O(n)$ space.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n \le 4$)

- **$n = 1$ ($2n = 2$ cells)**: The only opposite pair is $(0, 1)$, leaving arc length $L_1 = 0$. Sum of beauties $= \mathbf{0}$.
- **$n = 2$ ($2n = 4$ cells)**: To avoid $L_r = 0$, at most one opposite pair can be chosen, leaving two opposite arcs of odd length $L_1 = 1$. Neither an internal pair nor a valid distance-$2$ straddle can tile an arc of length $1$ on a $4$-cell circle. Sum of beauties $= \mathbf{0}$.
- **$n = 3$ ($2n = 6$ cells)**: To have $L_r \ge 1$, there must be exactly $m = 1$ opposite pair $(i_1, i_1 + 3)$ ($3$ rotational choices $i_1 \in \{0, 1, 2\}$), leaving two opposite arcs of length $L_1 = 2$ (beauty $L_1^2 = 4$). The $4$ remaining cells can be paired in $2$ ways: either two distance-$1$ pairs inside the two arcs, or two distance-$2$ pairs straddling across $i_1$ and $i_1 + 3$. Sum of beauties $= 3 \times 4 \times 2 = \mathbf{24}$.
- **$n = 4$ ($2n = 8$ cells)**: With $m = 1$ opposite pair, $L_1 = 3$ is odd and cannot be paired ($0$ ways). With $m = 2$ opposite pairs at distance $2$ ($2$ rotational placements $\{0, 2\}$ and $\{1, 3\}$), both arc lengths are $L_1 = L_2 = 1$ (beauty $1^2 \cdot 1^2 = 1$), and we must straddle across one of the two opposite pairs so that both arcs of length $1$ are consumed ($2$ choices of which opposite pair is straddled). Sum of beauties $= 2 \times 1 \times 2 = \mathbf{4}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

Consider a single linear segment of $L$ cells that contains no opposite pairs. If we match its cells using only distance-$1$ and distance-$2$ pairs, a distance-$1$ pair at the left end consumes $\{1, 2\}$ (length $2$), whereas a distance-$2$ pair $(1, 3)$ forces cell $2$ to pair with cell $4$, consuming $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ (an indivisible block of length $4$).

Now look at what happens at an opposite pair $(i_r, i_r + n)$: a distance-$2$ pair can also **straddle** across $i_r$ by matching $(i_r - 1, i_r + 1)$ (and by central symmetry, $(i_r + n - 1, i_r + n + 1)$). Such a straddle consumes $1$ cell from the right end of the preceding arc and $1$ cell from the left end of the following arc, without changing the beauty factor $L_r^2$ of either arc.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: Cutting the circle at the opposite pairs decomposes the matching into a cyclic sequence of steps $k_1 + k_2 + \dots + k_m = n$ (where $L_r = k_r - 1$ is the arc length between $i_r$ and $i_{r+1}$). At each opposite pair $i_r$, there is a binary boundary state $b_r \in \{0, 1\}$ indicating whether a distance-$2$ pair straddles across $i_r$.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 9 (§9.2 — Coupled Semi-Online Convolution via CDQ Divide-and-Conquer NTT)** (or **Chapter 5** rational matrix denominator clearing).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

Let $g_0 = 1, g_1 = 0, g_2 = 1, g_3 = 0$, and $g_m = g_{m-2} + g_{m-4}$ ($g_{2j} = F_{j+1}$, $g_{2j+1} = 0$) count the internal matchings of $m$ cells. For $c = b_{\text{left}} + b_{\text{right}} \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ straddled endpoints on an arc of step size $k \ge 1$ ($L = k - 1$ cells), define the three transition polynomials:
$$P_c(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (k - 1)^2 \, g_{k - 1 - c} \, x^k \qquad (c \in \{0, 1, 2\}),$$
where $g_m = 0$ for $m < 0$. Tracking the open chain OGFs $D_{a, b}(x)$ from initial boundary state $a \in \{0, 1\}$ to current boundary state $b \in \{0, 1\}$ gives the $2 \times 2$ coupled semi-online system:
$$\begin{bmatrix} D_{a, 0}(x) \\ D_{a, 1}(x) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} P_a(x) \\ P_{a+1}(x) \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} P_0(x) & P_1(x) \\ P_1(x) & P_2(x) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} D_{a, 0}(x) \\ D_{a, 1}(x) \end{bmatrix},$$
and rooting the cycle at the unique arc of step $k$ straddling cell $0$ (with rotational multiplicity $k$) yields:
$$\text{Ans} = [x^n] \sum_{k=1}^{n} k \, x^k \Big( (k-1)^2 g_{k-1} \big(1 + D_{0,0}(x)\big) + 2 (k-1)^2 g_{k-2} D_{0,1}(x) + (k-1)^2 g_{k-3} \big(1 + D_{1,1}(x)\big) \Big).$$

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.2` (`#131`) — Count BFS Graphs

- **Source**: [Codeforces 1906J — Count BFS Graphs](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1906/J) (2023–2024 ICPC Asia Jakarta Regional Contest, Problem J)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

You are given a permutation $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ with $a_1 = 1$. Consider the standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) traversal on a simple, connected, undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ with vertex set $V = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ starting from vertex $1$, where **whenever a vertex $u$ is popped from the front of the queue, all of its unvisited neighbors are pushed to the back of the queue in strictly increasing order of their vertex labels**:

```text
visited[1] = true; Q.push(1)
while Q is not empty:
    u = Q.pop_front()
    output.append(u)
    for v in sorted(neighbors(u)):
        if not visited[v]:
            visited[v] = true
            Q.push(v)
```

Count the number of simple undirected graphs $G$ on $\{1, \dots, n\}$ for which this BFS procedure visits all $n$ vertices and produces the exact output sequence $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, modulo $998244353$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 5000$ (Original Version) or $1 \le n \le 10^5$ (Strengthened Version), modulus $p = 998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n)$ space (or $O(n \log^2 n)$ for the strengthened version).

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n \le 4$)

- **$n = 1$, $a = [1]$**: Only $1$ graph on $1$ vertex. Output $= \mathbf{1}$.
- **$n = 2$, $a = [1, 2]$**: The edge $(1, 2)$ must be present ($1$ graph). Output $= \mathbf{1}$.
- **$n = 3$, $a = [1, 2, 3]$**:
  - If vertex $1$ pushes only $[2]$, then when $2$ is popped it must push $[3]$ ($1$ graph: path $1 - 2 - 3$).
  - If vertex $1$ pushes $[2, 3]$ (valid since $2 < 3$), then when $2$ is popped the queue already contains $3$, so the edge $(2, 3)$ can be either absent or present ($2^1 = 2$ graphs).
  - Total for $a = [1, 2, 3]$: $1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}$.
- **$n = 3$, $a = [1, 3, 2]$**:
  - Vertex $1$ cannot push $[3, 2]$ together because $3 > 2$ violates the sorted neighbor rule. Thus $1$ pushes only $[3]$, and then $3$ pushes $[2]$ ($1$ graph: path $1 - 3 - 2$).
  - Total for $a = [1, 3, 2]$: $\mathbf{1}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

At the moment vertex $a_i$ is popped from the queue, suppose the queue currently contains $a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, \dots, a_j$ (for some $j \ge i$). The newly discovered neighbors of $a_i$ are appended to the queue as a contiguous block $a_{j+1}, a_{j+2}, \dots, a_k$ ($k \ge j$).

Ask two questions about this step:
1. When can $a_{j+1}, \dots, a_k$ be pushed together by $a_i$? Precisely when $a_{j+1} < a_{j+2} < \dots < a_k$.
2. Which other vertices can $a_i$ have edges to without changing the BFS order? Vertex $a_i$ cannot connect to any unvisited vertex outside $\{a_{j+1}, \dots, a_k\}$, and edges to $a_1, \dots, a_{i-1}$ were already decided when those vertices were popped. What about edges between $a_i$ and the **already-queued** vertices $a_{i+1}, \dots, a_j$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: Each vertex $a_i$ has $2^{j - i}$ free edge choices to the already-queued segment $a[i+1 \dots j]$, and extends the queue tail from $j$ to $k$ across any strictly increasing subarray $a[j+1 \dots k]$.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 9 (§9.1 — Prefix/Interval-Sum Online DP Acceleration)** combined with **Chapter 13 (§13.1 — $2^{\binom{k}{2}}$ / $2^{j-i}$ Labeled Graphical Edge Factors)**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

Let $\text{dp}[i][k]$ be the number of valid edge configurations among the edges incident to $a_1, \dots, a_i$ such that after $a_i$ is processed, the queue spans $a[1 \dots k]$. Let $L[k]$ be the smallest index $\ge 2$ such that $a[L[k] \dots k]$ is strictly increasing. Then for $1 \le i \le k \le n$ (with $k > i$ whenever $i < n$ to keep the queue non-empty):
$$\text{dp}[i][k] = \sum_{j = \max(i,\, L[k] - 1)}^{k} 2^{j - i} \, \text{dp}[i - 1][j],$$
with base case $\text{dp}[1][k] = 1$ for all $2 \le k \le R[2]$ (where $a[2 \dots R[2]]$ is the maximal increasing prefix starting at index $2$). Scaling $\widetilde{\text{dp}}[i - 1][j] = 2^j \, \text{dp}[i - 1][j]$ reduces the transition for all $k$ to a single sliding range sum multiplied by $2^{-i}$.

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.3` (`#133`) — Counting Is Fun (Excursion-Majority Binary Strings)

- **Source**: Adapted from [Codeforces 1930I — Counting Is Fun](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1930/I) (think-cell Round 1, Problem I)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Consider a binary string $s = s_1 s_2 \dots s_{2n} \in \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}^{2n}$ of even length $2n$. Map $\mathtt{1} \mapsto +1$ and $\mathtt{0} \mapsto -1$, and let $S_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} (2 s_j - 1)$ be the prefix sums ($S_0 = 0$), with historical prefix minimum $M_k = \min_{0 \le l \le k} S_l$.

A step $i \in \{1, \dots, 2n\}$ is called a **record-low step** if $s_i = \mathtt{0}$ and $S_{i-1} = M_{i-1}$ (so $S_i = M_{i-1} - 1$ sets a new strict minimum $M_i = M_{i-1} - 1$). We say that $s \in \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}^{2n}$ is **excursion-majority good** if it satisfies two rules:

1. **Even Record-Low Depth**: The total number of record-low steps in $s$ is even ($2h$ for some integer $h \ge 0$, so the final minimum $M_{2n} = -2h$ has the same parity as $2n$, allowing the walk to return to or stay above $M_{2n}$).
2. **Local Excursion Recovery**: Every record-low step $i$ must be immediately followed (before the next record-low step, or before the end of the string if $i$ is the last record-low step) by at least one $\mathtt{1}$ step that lifts the walk back to $S_r \ge S_i + 1 = M_{i-1}$ (so every record-low $\mathtt{0}$ is locally covered by a balanced $\mathtt{0}\dots\mathtt{1}$ excursion above $M_i$).

Given $n$ and an **arbitrary prime modulus $p$** (which is **not** guaranteed to be NTT-friendly!), compute the number of excursion-majority good binary strings of length $2n$ modulo $p$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 5 \times 10^5$, $10^8 < p < 10^9 + 9$ is an arbitrary prime given in the input.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space, using **zero NTTs** and **zero divisions by $n$**.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n \le 4$)

- **$n = 1$ (length $2n = 2$, $4$ strings total)**:
  - With $2h = 0$ record lows ($S_k \ge 0$ for all $k$): $\mathtt{11}$ ($S = [0, 1, 2]$) and $\mathtt{10}$ ($S = [0, 1, 0]$) are valid ($2$ strings).
  - $\mathtt{01}$ has $1$ record low (odd), and $\mathtt{00}$ has $2$ record lows with no recovery after either.
  - Total for $n = 1$: $\mathbf{2}$.
- **$n = 2$ (length $2n = 4$, $16$ strings total)**:
  - Any valid string with $2h \ge 2$ record lows needs $2$ record-low $\mathtt{0}$ steps plus at least $2$ recovery steps after each, requiring length $\ge 6$. Thus for $n = 2$, only $2h = 0$ (walks of length $4$ with $S_k \ge 0$ for all $k$) can occur: $\mathtt{1111}, \mathtt{1110}, \mathtt{1101}, \mathtt{1100}, \mathtt{1011}, \mathtt{1010}$.
  - Total for $n = 2$: $\mathbf{6}$.
- **$n = 3$ (length $2n = 6$, $64$ strings total)**:
  - $2h = 0$: $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ walks of length $6$ with $S_k \ge 0$.
  - $2h = 2$: The first record low ($\mathtt{0}$ at $i=1$) is followed by $\mathtt{10}$ (recovering to $0$ and returning to $-1$), then the second record low ($\mathtt{0}$ at $i=4$, reaching $-2$) is followed by a recovery walk of length $2$ staying $\ge -2$, which must be $\mathtt{10}$ or $\mathtt{11}$. This gives $2$ strings: $\mathtt{010010}$ and $\mathtt{010011}$.
  - Total for $n = 3$: $20 + 2 = \mathbf{22}$.
- **$n = 4$ (length $2n = 8$, $256$ strings total)**:
  - $2h = 0$: $\binom{8}{4} = 70$ walks with $S_k \ge 0$.
  - $2h = 2$: $12$ valid strings (distributing the $3$ pairs of non-record steps among the pre-record excursion, the first recovery excursion, and the final recovery meander gives $2 + 4 + 6 = 12$).
  - Total for $n = 4$: $70 + 12 = \mathbf{82}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

Factor any valid walk $s \in \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}^{2n}$ at its $2h$ record-low steps $i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_{2h}$:
- Before $i_1$, the walk starts at $0$, stays $\ge 0$, and ends at $0$ (an even-length non-negative return walk).
- Between $i_r$ and $i_{r+1}$ ($1 \le r \le 2h - 1$), the walk starts at $-r$, stays $\ge -r$, ends at $-r$, and by Rule 2 must have **positive** length $\ge 2$.
- After $i_{2h}$, the walk starts at $-2h$, stays $\ge -2h$, has even length, and if $h \ge 1$ it must have **positive** length $\ge 2$.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: Every block between record lows is governed by the Catalan series $C(z) = 1 + z C(z)^2$ (where $z$ marks a pair of steps, i.e., semi-length $1$). Thus the OGF $F(z)$ is a rational function $R(u(z))$ of the shifted Catalan series $u(z) = C(z) - 1 = z C(z)^2$, which satisfies $u = z(1 + u)^2 \iff z = \frac{u}{(1+u)^2}$. Because the prime $p$ is arbitrary, we cannot use NTT; we need an exact $O(n)$ extraction in $u$-space.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 10 (§10.2 — Implicit Catalan Functional Equations)** combined with **Chapter 11 (§11.1–11.2 — Formal Residue Change of Variables / Canonical Form 4)**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

With $u = C(z) - 1$ satisfying $z = \frac{u}{(1+u)^2}$ and $dz = \frac{1-u}{(1+u)^3}\,du$, a full Dyck path has OGF $1 + u$, a non-empty Dyck path has OGF $u$, an even Dyck meander has OGF $\frac{1+u}{1-u}$, and a non-empty even meander has OGF $\frac{2u}{1-u}$. Summing over $h \ge 0$ pairs of record lows gives:
$$F(z) = R\big(u(z)\big) = \frac{1+u}{1-u} + (1+u) \sum_{h=1}^{\infty} z^h u^{2h-1} \frac{2u}{1-u} = \frac{1+u}{1-u}\left(1 + \frac{2u^3}{(1+u)^2 - u^3}\right).$$
Applying the Formal Residue Change-of-Variables theorem $[z^n] R(u(z)) = [u^n] \left(R(u) \frac{1-u}{1+u} (1+u)^{2n}\right)$ cancels $\frac{1+u}{1-u}$ completely, yielding:
$$[z^n] F(z) = [u^n] \left( \frac{1 + 2u + u^2 + u^3}{1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3} (1 + u)^{2n} \right) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} q_k \binom{2n}{n - k} \pmod{p},$$
where $q_0 = 1, q_1 = 0, q_2 = 0, q_3 = 2$, and $q_k = -2q_{k-1} - q_{k-2} + q_{k-3}$ for $k \ge 4$.

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.4` (`#160`) — Intrinsic Interval (Simple Permutations)

- **Source**: [Luogu P4747 — [CERC2017] Intrinsic Interval / Simple Permutations](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P4747)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

A permutation $\pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \dots, \pi_k)$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ has a **framed interval** (or **block**) on $[l \dots r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le k$) if the contiguous subarray $\pi[l \dots r]$ takes a contiguous set of values $\{\min \pi[l \dots r], \dots, \max \pi[l \dots r]\}$, i.e.,
$$\max_{l \le i \le r} \pi_i - \min_{l \le i \le r} \pi_i = r - l.$$
Every permutation of length $k$ trivially has blocks of length $1$ (singletons $[i, i]$) and length $k$ (the whole permutation $[1, k]$). A permutation $\pi \in S_k$ ($k \ge 4$) is called **simple** (or **interval-indecomposable**) if it has **no** block of length $m$ with $2 \le m \le k-1$.

Given $n$, compute the number $s_k$ of simple permutations of length $k$ for **every** $k \in \{4, 5, \dots, n\}$ modulo $998244353$.

- **Constraints**: $4 \le n \le 10^5$, modulus $p = 998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ (or $O(n \log^2 n)$) time and $O(n)$ space.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($k \le 5$)

- **$k = 1, 2, 3$**:
  - For $k = 2$, both $[1, 2]$ and $[2, 1]$ only have intervals of length $1$ and $2$, which are monotone two-element blocks rather than simple permutations of length $\ge 4$.
  - For $k = 3$, all $3! = 6$ permutations contain an adjacent pair of consecutive values ($\{1, 2\}$ or $\{2, 3\}$), i.e., a proper interval of length $2$. Thus $s_3 = \mathbf{0}$.
- **$k = 4$ ($4! = 24$ permutations)**:
  - Checking all $24$ permutations of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, $22$ of them contain a contiguous block of length $2$ or $3$, while exactly $s_4 = \mathbf{2}$ permutations have no proper intervals of length $2$ or $3$:
    $$\pi^{(1)} = [2, 4, 1, 3], \qquad \pi^{(2)} = [3, 1, 4, 2].$$
- **$k = 5$ ($5! = 120$ permutations)**:
  - Exhaustive check (or subtracting block inflations of $[1, 2]$, $[2, 1]$, and $[2, 4, 1, 3], [3, 1, 4, 2]$ from $5! = 120$) yields $s_5 = \mathbf{6}$ simple permutations of length $5$:
    $$[2, 4, 1, 5, 3],\; [2, 5, 3, 1, 4],\; [3, 1, 5, 2, 4],\; [3, 5, 1, 4, 2],\; [4, 1, 3, 5, 2],\; [4, 2, 5, 1, 3].$$

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Combinatorial Decomposition (Zero Spoilers)</summary>

Instead of directly counting permutations that *avoid* all non-trivial contiguous value blocks, consider how an arbitrary permutation $\pi \in S_n$ ($n \ge 2$) is built by inflating a smaller base permutation $\sigma \in S_m$ ($m \ge 2$) with $m$ contiguous value blocks $B_1, B_2, \dots, B_m$. When is this inflation decomposition unique, and what special case arises when $\sigma$ itself can be split into two monotone pieces?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: Translating the three disjoint inflation cases into ordinary generating functions relates the known factorial OGF $F(x) = \sum_{k \ge 1} k!\, x^k$ to the unknown simple-permutation OGF $S(y) = \sum_{k \ge 4} s_k y^k$ evaluated at $y = F(x)$. Solving for $S(y)$ requires the **compositional inverse** $G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y)$ satisfying $F(G(y)) = y$.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 10 (§10.2–10.3 — Implicit Functional Equations & Newton Iteration for Compositional Inverse)** (keeping strictly within Part III tools $\le \text{Ch } 13$).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

Let $F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} k!\, x^k$ be the OGF of non-empty permutations. An indecomposable block inside an ascending join has OGF $F_{\neq \text{asc}}(x) = \frac{F(x)}{1 + F(x)}$, so ascending joins of $m \ge 2$ parts have OGF $\sum_{m \ge 2} \left(\frac{F}{1+F}\right)^m = \frac{F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)}$, and likewise $\frac{F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)}$ for descending joins. Thus:
$$F(x) = x + \frac{2 F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)} + S\big(F(x)\big).$$
Setting $y = F(x) \iff x = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y) =: G(y)$ isolates $S(y)$ immediately:
$$S(y) = y - \frac{2y^2}{1 + y} - G(y) = \frac{y(1 - y)}{1 + y} - G(y),$$
where $G(y) \bmod y^{n+1}$ is computed by Newton iteration $G_{\text{next}}(y) = G(y) - \frac{F(G(y)) - y}{F'(G(y))} \bmod y^{2d}$.

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.5` (`#119`) — AmShZ Farm

- **Source**: [Codeforces 1528F — AmShZ Farm](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1528/F) (Codeforces Round 722, Div. 1, Problem F)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

There are $n$ parking spaces numbered $1, 2, \dots, n$ along a one-way street, and $n$ cars arrive one by one. Car $j$ ($1 \le j \le n$) has a preferred parking space $a_j \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$: upon arrival, it drives to space $a_j$ and parks in the first unoccupied space at an index $\ge a_j$ (if all spaces $a_j, a_j + 1, \dots, n$ are already occupied, car $j$ cannot park).

A preference sequence $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}^n$ is called **valid** if all $n$ cars successfully park; equivalently, for every $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, at least $i$ cars prefer a space $\le i$:
$$\big\lvert \{ j \in \{1, \dots, n\} : a_j \le i \} \big\rvert \ge i \qquad \forall\, i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}.$$
For a valid sequence $a$ and a spot $v \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, let $\operatorname{occ}(v, a) = \lvert \{ j : a_j = v \} \rvert$ denote the number of times $v$ appears in $a$. Given $n$ and $k$, compute:
$$\sum_{a \text{ valid}} \sum_{v=1}^{n} \big(\operatorname{occ}(v, a)\big)^k \pmod{998244353}.$$

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 10^9$, $1 \le k \le 10^5$, modulus $p = 998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(k \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ space.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n \le 3$)

- **$n = 1$, any $k \ge 1$**: Only $a = (1)$ is valid, with $\operatorname{occ}(1, a) = 1 \implies 1^k = \mathbf{1}$.
- **$n = 2$, $k = 2$**:
  - Among $\{1, 2\}^2$, the $3$ valid sequences are $(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)$ (only $(2, 2)$ fails because $0 < 1$ cars have $a_j \le 1$).
  - For $a = (1, 1)$: $\operatorname{occ}(1, a)^2 + \operatorname{occ}(2, a)^2 = 2^2 + 0^2 = 4$.
  - For $a = (1, 2)$: $1^2 + 1^2 = 2$.
  - For $a = (2, 1)$: $1^2 + 1^2 = 2$.
  - Total for $n = 2, k = 2$: $4 + 2 + 2 = \mathbf{8}$.
- **$n = 3$, $k = 2$**:
  - There are $(3 + 1)^{3 - 1} = 16$ valid sequences of length $3$.
  - Counting pairs $(a, v)$ by frequency $m = \operatorname{occ}(v, a) \in \{1, 2, 3\}$:
    - $m = 3$: only $a = (1, 1, 1), v = 1$ ($1$ pair, contributing $1 \times 3^2 = 9$).
    - $m = 2$: $9$ pairs $(a, v)$ (contributing $9 \times 2^2 = 36$).
    - $m = 1$: $27$ pairs $(a, v)$ (contributing $27 \times 1^2 = 27$).
  - Total for $n = 3, k = 2$: $9 + 36 + 27 = \mathbf{72}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

Add an extra parking space $n + 1$ and arrange all $n + 1$ spaces $1, 2, \dots, n + 1$ around a **circle** so that cars wrap around modulo $n + 1$. Now every sequence $a \in \{1, 2, \dots, n + 1\}^n$ allows all $n$ cars to park, leaving **exactly one empty space** on the circle!

If you shift every preference by $+1 \bmod (n + 1)$ (sending $a_j \mapsto (a_j \bmod (n+1)) + 1$), the empty space also shifts by $+1 \bmod (n + 1)$. Therefore, in every cyclic shift orbit of size $n + 1$, there is **exactly one** sequence whose empty space is $n + 1$ — which is precisely a valid parking sequence on $\{1, \dots, n\}$! Moreover, in that valid sequence, $\operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a) = 0$. What does this tell you about the multiset of frequencies $\{\operatorname{occ}(1, a), \dots, \operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a)\}$ across the entire orbit?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: By Pollak's circular symmetry / Raney's Cycle Lemma, each cyclic orbit of size $n + 1$ contributes the exact same nonzero frequency $k$-th powers $\sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k$ at its unique valid representative as the average over all $n + 1$ shifts in the orbit! Because $n \le 10^9$ is huge and $k \le 10^5$ is small, we convert $m^k$ into falling factorials $m^{\underline{j}}$ via Stirling numbers of the second kind.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 11 (§11.3 — Raney's Lemma & Circular Shift Orbit Bijection)** combined with **Chapter 6 (§6.4 — Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind & Binomial-Moment Collapse)**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

Summing $\sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k$ over all $(n + 1)^n$ unrestricted sequences $a \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\}^n$ and dividing by the orbit size $n + 1$ (since $\operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a) = 0$ on every valid parking sequence) gives:
$$\text{Ans} = \frac{1}{n + 1} \sum_{a \in \{1, \dots, n+1\}^n} \sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k = \sum_{m=1}^{n} \binom{n}{m} n^{n - m} \, m^k.$$
Expanding $m^k = \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} m^{\underline{j}}$ and using $\binom{n}{m} m^{\underline{j}} = n^{\underline{j}} \binom{n - j}{m - j}$ collapses the $n$-term sum into a $k$-term closed form:
$$\text{Ans} = \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} n^{\underline{j}} \, (n + 1)^{n - j} \pmod{998244353}.$$

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.6` (`#035`) — Sum of Prod of Min

- **Source**: [AtCoder Beginner Contest 279 Ex — Sum of Prod of Min](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc279/tasks/abc279_h)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Given positive integers $N$ and $M$ satisfying $N \le M \le 2N$, consider all ordered $N$-tuples of **positive** integers $(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}^N$ whose sum is $M$:
$$A_1 + A_2 + \dots + A_N = M.$$
Compute the sum of the products $\prod_{i=1}^{N} \min(i, A_i)$ over all such $N$-tuples:
$$\sum_{\substack{A_1 + \dots + A_N = M \\ A_1, \dots, A_N \ge 1}} \prod_{i=1}^{N} \min(i, A_i) \pmod{200003}.$$

- **Constraints**:
  - **Official Extreme-Scale Version**: $1 \le N \le 10^{12}$, $N \le M \le 2N$, prime modulus $P = 200003$.
  - **Generalized Cap Subtask**: Also analyze how to solve the version where the upper cap $\min(i, A_i)$ is replaced by $\min(B_i, A_i)$ for an arbitrary given positive integer array $B_1, \dots, B_N$ with $\sum_{i=1}^N B_i \le 2 \times 10^5$ modulo $998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O\big(P + \sqrt{M - N} \log_P M\big)$ time for the official $N \le 10^{12}$ problem; $O(N \log N)$ or $O(N \log^2 N)$ for arbitrary $B_i$ with $N, M \le 2 \times 10^5$.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($N \le 3$)

- **$N = 1, M = 2$**: Only $A = (2)$, with $\min(1, 2) = \mathbf{1}$.
- **$N = 2, M = 4$**: The $3$ compositions of $4$ into $2$ positive parts are:
  - $(3, 1) \mapsto \min(1, 3)\min(2, 1) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
  - $(2, 2) \mapsto \min(1, 2)\min(2, 2) = 1 \cdot 2 = 2$.
  - $(1, 3) \mapsto \min(1, 1)\min(2, 3) = 1 \cdot 2 = 2$.
  - Sum for $N = 2, M = 4$: $1 + 2 + 2 = \mathbf{5}$.
- **$N = 3, M = 5$**: The $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ compositions of $5$ into $3$ positive parts are:
  - $(3, 1, 1) \mapsto 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$.
  - $(2, 2, 1) \mapsto 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 2$.
  - $(2, 1, 2) \mapsto 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 = 2$.
  - $(1, 3, 1) \mapsto 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 2$.
  - $(1, 2, 2) \mapsto 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 4$.
  - $(1, 1, 3) \mapsto 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 3 = 3$.
  - Sum for $N = 3, M = 5$: $1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 3 = \mathbf{14}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

For a single term $A_i \ge 1$ capped at $i$, write out the sequence of weights $\min(i, 1), \min(i, 2), \min(i, 3), \dots$:
$$1,\, 2,\, 3,\, \dots,\, i - 1,\, i,\, i,\, i,\, i,\, \dots$$
Take the first difference of this sequence (subtracting each term from the next):
$$1,\, 1,\, 1,\, \dots,\, 1,\, 0,\, 0,\, 0,\, \dots \qquad (\text{exactly } i \text{ ones, followed by all zeros!}).$$
And taking the second difference leaves $+1$ at position $1$ and $-1$ at position $i + 1$, with $0$ everywhere else!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: Because the second difference of $\min(i, a)$ has only two nonzero terms, the single-factor OGF is $\sum_{a \ge 1} \min(i, a) x^a = \frac{x(1 - x^i)}{(1 - x)^2}$. Multiplying over $i = 1 \dots N$ and shifting by $x^N$ asks for $[x^{M - N}] (1 - x)^{-2N} \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i)$. Furthermore, the constraint $M \le 2N$ means $K := M - N \le N$, so the finite product $\prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i)$ agrees with the infinite Euler product $\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i)$ up to degree $K$!
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 3 (§3.2–3.3 — Sparse Product Grouping & Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem)** + **Chapter 6 (Lucas's Theorem $\bmod\, P$)** (and **Chapter 9 §9.1** D&C NTT / $\ln$-$\exp$ for arbitrary $B_i$).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

Let $K = M - N \le N$. Since $[x^k] \prod_{i=1}^{N} (1 - x^i) = [x^k] \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i)$ for all $0 \le k \le N$, Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem $\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^k x^{k(3k-1)/2}$ yields:
$$\text{Ans} = [x^K] \left( (1 - x)^{-2N} \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 - x^i) \right) = \sum_{\substack{k \in \mathbb{Z} \\ \omega_k := \frac{k(3k-1)}{2} \le K}} (-1)^k \binom{2N + K - \omega_k - 1}{2N - 1} \pmod{200003},$$
where each binomial coefficient is evaluated in $O(\log_P M)$ time via Lucas's Theorem after an $O(P)$ factorial precomputation.

</details>

### Problem `CP-III.7` (`#205`) — Cryptography Assignment 3 (Small-Characteristic Implicit Tree Power)

- **Source**: [Luogu P8555 — 密码学第三次小作业](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P8555)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Let $p$ be a **small prime** ($2 \le p \le 10^5$), and let $\Phi(u) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i u^i \in \mathbb{F}_p[u]$ be a polynomial of small degree $d \le 5$ with nonzero constant term $c_0 = \Phi(0) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

Consider the unique formal power series $F(x) \in x \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$ satisfying the scale-invariant implicit tree equation:
$$F(x) = x \, \Phi\big(F(x)\big).$$
Combinatorially, $[x^n] F(x)^k$ counts ordered forests of $k$ rooted plane trees on $n$ total vertices where each vertex with $i$ children receives weight $c_i \in \mathbb{F}_p$.

Given $n$, $k$, $p$, and the coefficients $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_d$, compute:
$$[x^n] \, F(x)^k \pmod{p}.$$

- **Constraints**: $1 \le k \le n \le 10^{18}$, $1 \le d \le 5$, $2 \le p \le 10^5$ is prime, $c_0 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. **Crucial Warning**: $n$ is up to $10^{18}$ while $p \le 10^5$, so **$p \mid n$ frequently occurs**!
- **Target Complexity**: $O\big(d p \log(dp) \log_p n\big)$ (or $O(d^2 p \log_p n)$) time and $O(dp)$ space.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 3, p = 3$)

- Suppose $p = 3$, $d = 2$, $\Phi(u) = 1 + u + u^2 \in \mathbb{F}_3[u]$ (Motzkin trees where each vertex has $0, 1,$ or $2$ children), $n = 3$, and $k = 1$.
- Expanding $F(x) = x(1 + F(x) + F(x)^2)$ term-by-term:
  - $[x^1] F(x) = 1$ (a single root leaf).
  - $[x^2] F(x) = [x^1](F(x) + F(x)^2) = 1 + 0 = 1$ (root with $1$ leaf child).
  - $[x^3] F(x) = [x^2](F(x) + F(x)^2) = [x^2]F(x) + [x^2]F(x)^2 = 1 + 1^2 = \mathbf{2} \pmod{3}$ (a chain of $3$ vertices, or a root with $2$ leaf children).

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

Look closely at the relation between the prime modulus $p \le 10^5$ and the target index $n \le 10^{18}$: since $p \ll n$, the target index $n$ can be a multiple of $p$ ($n \equiv 0 \pmod p$). Any extraction formula or differential recurrence that divides by $n$ (or by $1, 2, \dots, n$) will encounter a $0 / 0$ division-by-zero singularity in $\mathbb{F}_p$. How can you formulate the coefficient extraction of $[x^n] F(x)^k$ from $F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))$ using only operations that never divide by $n$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: We have $F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p \le 10^5 \ll n \le 10^{18}$. Two standard tools fail when $p \le n$:
  1. Classical LIF $\frac{k}{n}[u^{n-k}]\Phi(u)^n$ fails whenever $p \mid n$.
  2. Computing $\Phi(u)^m$ via $\exp(m \ln \Phi(u))$ fails because $\ln$ and $\exp$ divide by $p, 2p, \dots \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 11 (§11.4 — Characteristic-$p$ Derivative-Free Lagrange Inversion & Base-$p$ Frobenius Digit Decimation)**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

By Derivative-Free Lagrange Inversion (Form 3 / Variant B), over **any** commutative ring (including $\mathbb{F}_p$ when $p \mid n$):
$$[x^n] F(x)^k = [u^{n-k}] \Big( \big(\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)\big) \, \Phi(u)^{n-1} \Big).$$
Let $A_0(u) := \Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)$ (degree $\le d$), $K := n - k$, and $M := n - 1$. By the Frobenius endomorphism over $\mathbb{F}_p$, $\Phi(u)^p \equiv \Phi(u^p) \pmod p$. Writing $K = p K' + k_0$ and $M = p M' + m_0$ with $k_0, m_0 \in \{0, \dots, p - 1\}$, we have:
$$[u^{p K' + k_0}] \Big( A(u) \, \Phi(u)^{m_0} \, \Phi(u^p)^{M'} \Big) = [u^{K'}] \Big( A_{\text{next}}(u) \, \Phi(u)^{M'} \Big),$$
where $A_{\text{next}}(u) = \sum_{j \ge 0} \big([u^{p j + k_0}] \, A(u) \Phi(u)^{m_0}\big) u^j$ also has degree $\le d$! Repeating this $O(\log_p n)$ times extracts the exact answer.

</details>

---

### Problem `CP-III.8` (`#163`) — Counting Trees (`[WC2019] 数树`)

- **Source**: [Luogu P5206 — [WC2019] 数树](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P5206) (NOI Winter Camp 2019, by Elegia / 吕欣)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Let $\mathcal{T}_n$ be the set of all $n^{n-2}$ labeled spanning trees on the vertex set $V = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. For any two labeled trees $T_1 = (V, E(T_1))$ and $T_2 = (V, E(T_2))$, if we merge every pair of vertices connected by a **shared edge** $e \in E(T_1) \cap E(T_2)$ into a single component and assign one of $y$ colors to each resulting connected component, there are $y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert}$ valid colorings.

You are given $n$, a weight $y \in [0, 998244353)$, and a subtask mode $\text{op} \in \{0, 1, 2\}$:

- **Mode $\text{op} = 0$**: Both trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ are given in the input. Compute $y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} \pmod{998244353}$.
- **Mode $\text{op} = 1$**: Tree $T_1$ is given in the input, while $T_2$ ranges over all $n^{n-2}$ labeled trees in $\mathcal{T}_n$. Compute:
  $$\sum_{T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n} y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} \pmod{998244353}.$$
- **Mode $\text{op} = 2$**: Neither tree is fixed; both $T_1$ and $T_2$ range independently over all $n^{n-2}$ labeled trees in $\mathcal{T}_n$. Compute:
  $$\sum_{T_1 \in \mathcal{T}_n} \sum_{T_2 \in \mathcal{T}_n} y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert} \pmod{998244353}.$$

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 10^5$, $0 \le y < 998244353$, $\text{op} \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, modulus $p = 998244353$.
- **Target Complexity**: $O(n)$ (or $O(n \log n)$) for $\text{op} = 0$; $O(n)$ for $\text{op} = 1$; $O(n \log n)$ for $\text{op} = 2$.

#### Small Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 3$)

For $n = 3$, there are $3^{3-2} = 3$ labeled trees on $\{1, 2, 3\}$: $T^{(1)} = \{(1,2), (2,3)\}$, $T^{(2)} = \{(1,3), (2,3)\}$, and $T^{(3)} = \{(1,2), (1,3)\}$.
- **Mode $\text{op} = 0$** (say $T_1 = T^{(1)}, T_2 = T^{(2)}$): They share $1$ edge $(2, 3)$, so the answer is $y^{3 - 1} = \mathbf{y^2}$.
- **Mode $\text{op} = 1$** (fix $T_1 = T^{(1)}$):
  - $T_2 = T^{(1)}$ shares $2$ edges $\implies y^{3 - 2} = y$.
  - $T_2 = T^{(2)}$ and $T_2 = T^{(3)}$ each share $1$ edge with $T_1 \implies 2 \cdot y^{3 - 1} = 2y^2$.
  - Total for $\text{op} = 1$: $\mathbf{y + 2y^2}$.
- **Mode $\text{op} = 2$** (sum over all $9$ pairs $(T_1, T_2)$):
  - By symmetry among the $3$ isomorphic trees $T^{(1)}, T^{(2)}, T^{(3)}$, the sum is $3(y + 2y^2) = \mathbf{3y + 6y^2}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Structural Observation (Spoiler-Free)</summary>

First check the special case $y = 1$, where every tree pair $(T_1, T_2)$ receives weight $1$.

For $y \neq 1$, directly counting pairs of trees whose edge intersection is **equal** to a given set $S$ is difficult because you must forbid all other edges from being shared. How can you rewrite the weight $y^{n - \lvert E(T_1) \cap E(T_2) \rvert}$ as a sum over edge subsets $S$ that are merely **contained in** $E(T_1) \cap E(T_2)$? Once $S$ is fixed, what kind of graph is $S$, and how do its connected components constrain $T_1$ and $T_2$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Diagnostic Signal & Paradigm Selection</summary>

- **Diagnostic Signal**: By the Generalized Cayley / Symbolic Matrix-Tree Forest-Completion Theorem, a spanning forest $S$ with $k = n - \lvert S \rvert$ connected components of sizes $s_1, \dots, s_k$ is contained in exactly $n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i$ labeled trees!
  - In $\text{op} = 1$, $S \subseteq E(T_1)$ is chosen by deleting $k - 1$ edges of the given tree $T_1$, and $\prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i$ counts ways to mark one vertex in each component via a $2$-state tree DP on $T_1$ in $O(n)$ time.
  - In $\text{op} = 2$, $S$ must be a forest in **both** $T_1$ and $T_2$; summing over all forests $S$ gives component weight $\propto s_i^{s_i - 2} \cdot s_i \cdot s_i = s_i^{s_i}$, so the total sum is an unlabeled `SET` of labeled tree components, solved by a single polynomial $\exp$ in $O(n \log n)$ time!
- **Target Paradigm**: **Chapter 13 (§13.4 — Symbolic Matrix-Tree Determinant Calculus & Generalized Cayley Forest Completion)** + **Chapter 4 / Chapter 8 (Binomial Subset Expansion & EGF Exponential Formula)**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Key Algebraic Equation</summary>

For $y \neq 1$:
- **Mode $\text{op} = 1$**: Using $\lvert S \rvert = n - k$, we have:
  $$\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=1} = y^n \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} (y^{-1} - 1)^{n - k} n^{k - 2} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i = \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^2} \sum_{S \subseteq E(T_1)} \prod_{i=1}^{k} \left( \frac{n y}{1 - y} \, s_i \right),$$
  which is evaluated in $O(n)$ time by a 2-state tree DP (`dp[u][0/1]`) on $T_1$.
- **Mode $\text{op} = 2$**: A vertex subset of size $s$ forms $s^{s-2}$ internal trees in $S$, and receives factor $s$ from completing $T_1$ and factor $s$ from completing $T_2$. By the Exponential Formula (`SET`),
  $$\text{Ans}_{\text{op}=2} = \frac{(1 - y)^n}{n^4} \, n! \, [x^n] \exp\!\left( \sum_{s=1}^{n} \frac{n^2 y}{1 - y} \frac{s^s}{s!} x^s \right) \pmod{998244353}.$$

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete Solution — CP-III.1 (#090: Codeforces 848E — Days of Floral Colours)</summary>

#### 1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & Combinatorial Reduction

We want to count centrally symmetric matchings of $2n$ circular cells into pairs of circular distance $1, 2,$ or $n$, weighted by the product of the lengths of the contiguous arcs remaining after all opposite pairs (distance $n$) are removed.

1. **Folding the Circle by Central Symmetry**:
   Number the cells $0, 1, \dots, 2n - 1$. An opposite pair matches $(i, i + n)$ for some $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$. Suppose a valid matching contains $m \ge 1$ opposite pairs at indices $0 \le i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_m < n$ (along with their antipodal partners $i_r + n$).
   Let $k_r = i_{r+1} - i_r \ge 1$ (with $i_{m+1} := i_1 + n$) be the circular step distances between consecutive opposite pairs along the upper semicircle, so $\sum_{r=1}^{m} k_r = n$.
   Removing the $m$ opposite pairs leaves $m$ upper arcs of lengths $L_r = k_r - 1$ and $m$ antipodal lower arcs of the exact same lengths $L_r = k_r - 1$. Thus the beauty of the matching is:
   $$\text{Beauty} = \prod_{r=1}^{m} L_r^2 = \prod_{r=1}^{m} (k_r - 1)^2.$$
   In particular, any step with $k_r = 1$ ($L_r = 0$) contributes $0$ to the beauty product, so we only need to consider steps $k_r \ge 2$.

2. **Internal Tiling of an Arc & Endpoint Straddles**:
   Because the matching is centrally symmetric, the pairing of the lower semicircle is the exact $+n$ image of the pairing of the upper semicircle. What can happen to the cells on the upper semicircle?
   - Across each opposite pair $i_r$, we may optionally place a **straddling distance-$2$ pair** $(i_r - 1, i_r + 1)$ (together with its symmetric image $(i_r + n - 1, i_r + n + 1)$). Let $b_r \in \{0, 1\}$ be the indicator of whether $i_r$ is straddled.
   - Inside the $r$-th upper arc (which has $L_r = k_r - 1$ cells), the straddles at its left endpoint $i_r$ and right endpoint $i_{r+1}$ consume $c_r = b_r + b_{r+1} \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ boundary cells, leaving $m_r = k_r - 1 - c_r$ internal cells (note that the left and right straddles are disjoint whenever $m_r \ge 0$).
   - How many ways $g_m$ can a contiguous linear segment of $m$ cells be partitioned into pairs of distance $1$ or $2$?
     - For $m = 0$, the empty segment has $g_0 = 1$ matching.
     - For odd $m$, $g_m = 0$ since every pair consumes $2$ cells.
     - For even $m \ge 2$, cell $1$ must pair either with cell $2$ (distance $1$, leaving $m - 2$ cells) or with cell $3$ (distance $2$, which forces cell $2$ to pair with cell $4$ since $1$ and $3$ are taken, consuming an indivisible block $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ of length $4$ and leaving $m - 4$ cells).
     Hence $g_m$ satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence on even indices:
     $$g_0 = 1, \quad g_1 = 0, \quad g_2 = 1, \quad g_3 = 0, \quad g_m = g_{m-2} + g_{m-4} \quad (m \ge 4),$$
     with $g_m = 0$ for $m < 0$.

#### 2. Coupled Semi-Online System & Circular Closure

For each $c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, define the transition generating function for a single step $k \ge 1$ with $c$ straddled endpoints:
$$P_c(x) = \sum_{k=2}^{n} (k - 1)^2 \, g_{k - 1 - c} \, x^k \qquad (c \in \{0, 1, 2\}).$$
Note that $[x^0] P_c(x) = [x^1] P_c(x) = 0$, so $\operatorname{val}(P_c) \ge 2$.
For a linear chain of one or more steps starting with left boundary state $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and ending with right boundary state $b \in \{0, 1\}$, let $D_{a, b}(x)$ be its OGF. Conditioning on the last step (which transitions from an intermediate boundary state $s \in \{0, 1\}$ to $b$ with weight $P_{s + b}(x)$, or consists of a single step of weight $P_{a + b}(x)$) yields the coupled semi-online system:
$$\begin{aligned}
D_{a, 0}(x) &= P_a(x) + P_0(x) D_{a, 0}(x) + P_1(x) D_{a, 1}(x), \\
D_{a, 1}(x) &= P_{a+1}(x) + P_1(x) D_{a, 0}(x) + P_2(x) D_{a, 1}(x),
\end{aligned} \qquad (a \in \{0, 1\}).$$
By reversal symmetry of the steps, $D_{0, 1}(x) = D_{1, 0}(x)$, so there are only **three** distinct series: $D_0(x) := D_{0, 0}(x)$, $D_1(x) := D_{0, 1}(x) = D_{1, 0}(x)$, and $D_2(x) := D_{1, 1}(x)$, satisfying:
$$\begin{aligned}
D_0(x) &= P_0(x) + P_0(x) D_0(x) + P_1(x) D_1(x), \\
D_1(x) &= P_1(x) + P_1(x) D_0(x) + P_2(x) D_1(x), \\
D_2(x) &= P_2(x) + P_1(x) D_1(x) + P_2(x) D_2(x).
\end{aligned}$$

To close the cycle of length $n$, focus on the unique step of length $k \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ that straddles cell $0$ (or starts at cell $0$). A step of length $k$ has **$k$ rotational placements** covering cell $0$:
- If $k = n$ ($m = 1$ opposite pair, so both endpoints of the single arc are the same opposite pair $b_1 \in \{0, 1\}$, giving $c = 2b_1 \in \{0, 2\}$), its contribution is:
  $$n \cdot \big( [x^n] P_0(x) + [x^n] P_2(x) \big) = n (n - 1)^2 (g_{n - 1} + g_{n - 3}).$$
- If $2 \le k \le n - 2$ ($m \ge 2$ opposite pairs), choosing the boundary states $(b_{\text{left}}, b_{\text{right}}) \in \{0, 1\}^2$ of the distinguished step of length $k$ and concatenating with an open chain of total length $n - k$ gives:
  $$\sum_{k=2}^{n-2} k \Big( [x^k] P_0(x) \cdot [x^{n-k}] D_0(x) + 2 [x^k] P_1(x) \cdot [x^{n-k}] D_1(x) + [x^k] P_2(x) \cdot [x^{n-k}] D_2(x) \Big).$$

#### 3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 3, 4$)

- Write out $P_c(x)$ up to $x^4$ using $g_0 = 1, g_1 = 0, g_2 = 1, g_3 = 0$:
  - $P_0(x) = 1^2 g_1 x^2 + 2^2 g_2 x^3 + 3^2 g_3 x^4 = 4 x^3$.
  - $P_1(x) = 1^2 g_0 x^2 + 2^2 g_1 x^3 + 3^2 g_2 x^4 = x^2 + 9 x^4$.
  - $P_2(x) = 1^2 g_{-1} x^2 + 2^2 g_0 x^3 + 3^2 g_1 x^4 = 4 x^3$.
- Thus up to $x^2$, $D_0(x) \equiv 0$, $D_1(x) \equiv x^2$, $D_2(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{x^3}$.
- For **$n = 3$**: only the $k = 3$ single-arc term contributes: $3 \cdot ([x^3]P_0 + [x^3]P_2) = 3 \cdot (4 + 4) = \mathbf{24}$.
- For **$n = 4$**: the $k = 4$ term is $4 \cdot (0 + 0) = 0$, and the $k = 2$ term is $2 \cdot \big(0 + 2 [x^2]P_1 \cdot [x^2]D_1 + 0\big) = 2 \cdot (2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1) = \mathbf{4}$. Both match Stage 1!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Failure Mode & Remedy: Naive $3 \times 3$ Convolutions vs. Point-Value Reuse in Coupled CDQ NTT

- **Failure Mode**: Treating the coupled system for $(D_0, D_1, D_2)$ as $6$ separate polynomial multiplications at every CDQ divide-and-conquer node $[l, r)$ performs $12$ forward NTTs and $6$ inverse NTTs of length $L = r - l$, tripling the constant factor.
- **Remedy**: At each CDQ node $[l, r)$ with midpoint $mid = \lfloor(l + r)/2\rfloor$, perform **only $3$ forward NTTs** on the left slices $\widehat{D}_0[l \dots mid), \widehat{D}_1[l \dots mid), \widehat{D}_2[l \dots mid)$ and **only $3$ forward NTTs** on the prefix slices $\widehat{P}_0[0 \dots L), \widehat{P}_1[0 \dots L), \widehat{P}_2[0 \dots L)$, compute the $3$ linear combinations pointwise in the frequency domain, and perform **only $3$ inverse NTTs**!
  *(Bonus Observation)*: Because $G(x) = \sum_{m \ge 0} g_m x^m = \frac{1}{1 - x^2 - x^4}$ is rational of degree $4$, each $P_c(x)$ is rational with denominator $(1 - x^2 - x^4)^3$ of degree $12$; clearing denominators reduces the entire system to a constant-coefficient linear recurrence solvable in $O(n)$ time!
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm Contract: Coupled Semi-Online CDQ NTT (`CF 848E`)

- **Input**: Integer $n \in [1, 5 \times 10^4]$.
- **Preconditions**: Modulus $p = 998244353$; $P_0(0) = P_1(0) = P_2(0) = 0$.
- **Output**: Total beauty modulo $998244353$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n \log^2 n)$ time ($9$ NTTs of size $L$ per CDQ interval of length $L$) and $O(n)$ space.
- **Core Invariant**: When `cdq(l, r)` is entered, $D_c[l \dots mid)$ already holds the exact coefficients $[x^i] D_c(x)$ for $l \le i < mid$, and the frequency-domain update adds the exact contribution of all pairs $(i, j)$ with $i \in [l, mid)$ and $i + j \in [mid, r)$.
:::

```cpp
void cdq(int l, int r) {
    if (r - l <= 64) {
        for (int i = l; i < r; ++i)
            for (int j = 2; i + j < r; ++j) {
                D0[i + j] = (D0[i + j] + D0[i] * P0[j] + D1[i] * P1[j]) % MOD;
                D1[i + j] = (D1[i + j] + D0[i] * P1[j] + D1[i] * P2[j]) % MOD;
                D2[i + j] = (D2[i + j] + D1[i] * P1[j] + D2[i] * P2[j]) % MOD;
            }
        return;
    }
    int mid = (l + r) >> 1;
    cdq(l, mid); apply_coupled_transition(l, mid, r); cdq(mid, r);
}
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete Solution — CP-III.2 (#131: Codeforces 1906J — Count BFS Graphs)</summary>

#### 1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & Queue-Tail Invariant

In a BFS starting at $a_1 = 1$, vertices enter the queue in the exact order $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ and are popped in that same order. Let us trace the state of the queue at the moment the $i$-th vertex $a_i$ is popped:

1. **Queue State Before Popping $a_i$**:
   Because $a_1, \dots, a_{i-1}$ have already been popped and processed, the vertices that have been discovered so far form a contiguous prefix $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_j$ of the array $a$, where $j \ge i$ (so the queue right after $a_i$ is popped consists of $a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}, \dots, a_j$).
2. **Newly Discovered Neighbors of $a_i$**:
   When $a_i$ is popped, all of its unvisited neighbors are pushed to the back of the queue in strictly increasing order of their labels. Thus, the newly pushed neighbors of $a_i$ must form the next contiguous block $a_{j+1}, a_{j+2}, \dots, a_k$ (for some $k \ge j$), and this block is valid if and only if it is **strictly increasing**:
   $$a_{j+1} < a_{j+2} < \dots < a_k.$$
   (If $k = j$, the block is empty, which is always vacuously increasing.)
3. **Counting All Edges Incident to $a_i$**:
   - **Edges from $a_i$ to $a_1, \dots, a_{i-1}$**: Already determined when $a_1, \dots, a_{i-1}$ were popped.
   - **Edges from $a_i$ to $a_{j+1}, \dots, a_k$**: All $k - j$ edges **must** be present (since these are the unvisited vertices discovered by $a_i$).
   - **Edges from $a_i$ to $a_{k+1}, \dots, a_n$**: All $n - k$ edges **must** be absent (otherwise $a_i$ would have discovered them now!).
   - **Edges from $a_i$ to $a_{i+1}, \dots, a_j$**: Because $a_{i+1}, \dots, a_j$ were **already in the queue** before $a_i$ was popped, adding or omitting an edge between $a_i$ and any vertex in $\{a_{i+1}, \dots, a_j\}$ has **zero effect** on the queue order! Since there are $j - i$ such vertices, there are **$2^{j - i}$ independent choices** for these edges.

#### 2. Algebraic Recurrence & Sliding Interval-Sum Linearization

For each $k \in \{2, \dots, n\}$, precompute the **leftmost increasing-run boundary** $L[k] \in \{2, \dots, k\}$ defined by:
$$L[k] = \begin{cases} 2 & \text{if } k = 2, \\ L[k - 1] & \text{if } k > 2 \text{ and } a_{k - 1} < a_k, \\ k & \text{if } k > 2 \text{ and } a_{k - 1} > a_k. \end{cases}$$
Then the subarray $a[j + 1 \dots k]$ ($j < k$) is strictly increasing if and only if $j + 1 \ge L[k]$, i.e., $j \ge L[k] - 1$ (and for $j = k$, the empty subarray is always valid).

Let $\text{dp}[i][k]$ be the number of valid edge choices incident to $a_1, \dots, a_i$ such that after $a_i$ pushes its new neighbors, the discovered prefix is $a[1 \dots k]$.
- **Base case ($i = 1$)**: Vertex $a_1 = 1$ starts with $j = 1$ and must push a non-empty increasing prefix $a[2 \dots k]$ (so $L[k] = 2$), giving $\text{dp}[1][k] = [L[k] = 2]$ for $2 \le k \le n$.
- **Transition ($2 \le i \le n$)**: For the graph to be connected, before $a_i$ is popped, at least $a_i$ itself must already be in the queue, so $j \ge i$. Summing over all valid prior queue tails $j \in [\max(i, L[k] - 1),\, k]$ gives:
  $$\text{dp}[i][k] = \sum_{j = \max(i,\, L[k] - 1)}^{k} 2^{j - i} \, \text{dp}[i - 1][j] = 2^{-i} \sum_{j = \max(i,\, L[k] - 1)}^{k} \Big( 2^j \, \text{dp}[i - 1][j] \Big).$$
  Defining the scaled prefix sums $P_{i-1}[r] = \sum_{j=1}^{r} 2^j \, \text{dp}[i - 1][j] \pmod{998244353}$ evaluates each state $\text{dp}[i][k]$ in $O(1)$ time:
  $$\text{dp}[i][k] = 2^{-i} \Big( P_{i-1}[k] - P_{i-1}\big[\max(i,\, L[k] - 1) - 1\big] \Big) \pmod{998244353}.$$
- **Final Answer**: $\text{dp}[n][n] \pmod{998244353}$ (or equivalently $\sum_{j=1}^{n} 2^{\binom{n - j}{2}} \text{dp}[j][n]$ if stopping as soon as $k = n$ is reached, since once all $n$ vertices are queued at step $j$, the remaining $n - j$ vertices $a_{j+1}, \dots, a_n$ have $\sum_{i=j+1}^{n} (n - i) = \binom{n - j}{2}$ completely free internal edges!).

#### 3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 3$)

- **Case 1: $a = [1, 2, 3]$** ($L[2] = 2, L[3] = 2$):
  - $i = 1$: $\text{dp}[1][2] = 1,\; \text{dp}[1][3] = 1$.
  - $i = 2$:
    - $\text{dp}[2][2] = 2^0 \text{dp}[1][2] = 1$.
    - $\text{dp}[2][3] = 2^{2-2} \text{dp}[1][2] + 2^{3-2} \text{dp}[1][3] = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 1 = 3$.
  - $i = 3$: $\text{dp}[3][3] = 2^{3-3} \text{dp}[2][3] = \mathbf{3}$.
- **Case 2: $a = [1, 3, 2]$** ($L[2] = 2, L[3] = 3$ since $3 > 2$):
  - $i = 1$: $\text{dp}[1][2] = 1,\; \text{dp}[1][3] = 0$.
  - $i = 2$: $\text{dp}[2][2] = 1$, and for $k = 3$, $\max(2, L[3] - 1) = 2$, so $\text{dp}[2][3] = 2^0 \text{dp}[1][2] + 2^1 \text{dp}[1][3] = 1 + 0 = 1$.
  - $i = 3$: $\text{dp}[3][3] = \mathbf{1}$. Both match Stage 1!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Failure Mode & Remedy: Forgetting the Empty-Push Case ($j = k$) When $a_{k-1} > a_k$

- **Failure Mode**: If $a_{k-1} > a_k$ (so $L[k] = k$), a common bug is to think that vertex $a_i$ can only reach state $k$ by pushing the single element $a_k$ ($j = k - 1$), overlooking $j = k$ (where $a_k$ was **already** pushed by an earlier vertex $a_{i'}$, and $a_i$ pushes **zero** new neighbors!).
- **Remedy**: Notice that $L[k] - 1 = k - 1 < k$, so our lower bound $\max(i, L[k] - 1)$ automatically includes both $j = k - 1$ (pushing the single element $[a_k]$) and $j = k$ (pushing the empty list $[]$). Never restrict $j$ to $j < k$ when $k \ge i$!
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm Contract: Scaled Prefix-Sum BFS Queue DP (`CF 1906J`)

- **Input**: Integer $n \ge 1$ and permutation $a_1, \dots, a_n$ with $a_1 = 1$.
- **Preconditions**: Modulus $p = 998244353$; $a$ is a permutation of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with $a_1 = 1$.
- **Output**: Number of valid simple undirected graphs modulo $998244353$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n)$ space using rolling arrays.
- **Core Invariant**: After iteration $i$, `dp[k]` ($i \le k \le n$) equals the exact number of choices for all edges incident to $\{a_1, \dots, a_i\}$ such that the union of neighborhoods of $\{a_1, \dots, a_i\}$ is $a[1 \dots k]$ and every vertex's newly discovered neighbors appear as a sorted contiguous block.
:::

```cpp
vector<long long> dp(n + 1, 0), pref(n + 1, 0);
for (int k = 2; k <= n && (k == 2 || a[k - 1] < a[k]); ++k) dp[k] = 1;
for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; ++j)
        pref[j] = (pref[j - 1] + dp[j] * pw2[j]) % MOD;
    fill(dp.begin(), dp.end(), 0);
    for (int k = i; k <= n; ++k) {
        int lo = max(i, L[k] - 1);
        long long sum = (pref[k] - pref[lo - 1] + MOD) % MOD;
        dp[k] = sum * inv_pw2[i] % MOD;
    }
}
long long ans = (n == 1) ? 1 : dp[n];
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete Solution — CP-III.3 (#133: Codeforces 1930I — Counting Is Fun)</summary>

#### 1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & Catalan Excursion Grammar

We want to count binary strings $s \in \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\}^{2n}$ of even length $2n$ modulo an **arbitrary prime $p$** such that the number of record-low steps is even ($2h$) and every record-low step is followed by a recovery walk before the next record low (or the end of the string).

1. **Decomposing at the $2h$ Record-Low Steps**:
   Let $z$ mark a **pair of steps** (length $2$, so we seek $[z^n] F(z)$). Recall that a **Dyck path** (starts at $0$, stays $\ge 0$, ends at $0$) has OGF $C(z) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4z}}{2z} = 1 + z C(z)^2$.
   Introduce the **shifted Catalan parameter** (`Ch 10 §10.2` / `Ch 11 §11.2`):
   $$u = u(z) := C(z) - 1 = z C(z)^2 \implies u = z (1 + u)^2 \iff z = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2}.$$
   Let us express every building block of our walk in terms of $u$:
   - **Unrestricted Dyck path** (length $\ge 0$, stays $\ge 0$, returns to $0$):
     $$C(z) = 1 + u.$$
   - **Non-empty Dyck path** (length $\ge 2$, starts with $\mathtt{1}$, stays $\ge 0$, returns to $0$):
     $$C(z) - 1 = u.$$
   - **Even-length Dyck meander** (starts at $0$, stays $\ge 0$, ends at any even height $2r \ge 0$):
     Decomposing at the last visits to levels $0, 1, \dots, 2r - 1$ gives $C(z) \big(z C(z)^2\big)^r = (1 + u) u^r$. Summing over $r \ge 0$ yields:
     $$M(z) = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (1 + u) u^r = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u} = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \binom{2m}{m} z^m.$$
   - **Non-empty even-length Dyck meander** (length $\ge 2$, starts with $\mathtt{1}$, stays $\ge 0$, ends at $2r \ge 0$):
     $$M(z) - 1 = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u} - 1 = \frac{2u}{1 - u}.$$

2. **Assembling the Full OGF $F(z) = R(u(z))$**:
   - **Case $h = 0$ ($0$ record-low steps)**: The walk never dips below $0$, so it is an unrestricted even-length Dyck meander with OGF $\frac{1 + u}{1 - u}$.
   - **Case $h \ge 1$ ($2h$ record-low steps)**:
     - Before the $1$-st record-low step, the walk performs a Dyck path at level $0$: weight $1 + u$.
     - The $2h$ record-low $\mathtt{0}$-steps themselves contribute $z^h$.
     - After each of the first $2h - 1$ record-low steps, Rule 2 requires a **non-empty** Dyck path returning to that record-low level: weight $u^{2h - 1}$.
     - After the $2h$-th record-low step, Rule 2 requires a **non-empty** even-length Dyck meander staying $\ge -2h$: weight $\frac{2u}{1 - u}$.
   Summing over $h = 0$ and all $h \ge 1$ gives:
   $$F(z) = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u} + (1 + u) \sum_{h=1}^{\infty} z^h u^{2h - 1} \frac{2u}{1 - u}.$$
   Substitute $z = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2}$ into the geometric ratio $z u^2 = \frac{u^3}{(1 + u)^2}$:
   $$\sum_{h=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{u^3}{(1 + u)^2}\right)^h = \frac{\frac{u^3}{(1 + u)^2}}{1 - \frac{u^3}{(1 + u)^2}} = \frac{u^3}{(1 + u)^2 - u^3}.$$
   Therefore, $F(z) = R(u(z))$ where $R(u)$ is the rational function:
   $$R(u) = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u} \left( 1 + \frac{2 u^3}{(1 + u)^2 - u^3} \right) = \frac{1 + u}{1 - u} \cdot \frac{1 + 2u + u^2 + u^3}{1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3}.$$

#### 2. Formal Residue Change of Variables for Arbitrary Prime $p$

Because $p$ is an **arbitrary prime** given in the input, we cannot use NTT or divide by $n$. Instead, we apply the **Formal Residue Change-of-Variables Formula** (`Ch 11 §11.1–11.2`):
Since $z = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2}$ has valuation $1$, its formal differential is:
$$dz = \frac{(1 + u)^2 - 2u(1 + u)}{(1 + u)^4}\,du = \frac{1 - u}{(1 + u)^3}\,du.$$
Extracting $[z^n] F(z) = \operatorname{res}_z \big(F(z) z^{-n-1}\,dz\big)$ via the residue invariance theorem yields:
$$\begin{aligned}
[z^n] F(z) &= \operatorname{res}_u \left( R(u) \left(\frac{(1 + u)^2}{u}\right)^{n+1} \frac{1 - u}{(1 + u)^3}\,du \right) \\
&= [u^n] \left( R(u) \frac{1 - u}{1 + u} (1 + u)^{2n} \right).
\end{aligned}$$
Look at the product $Q(u) := R(u) \frac{1 - u}{1 + u}$: the prefactor $\frac{1 + u}{1 - u}$ in $R(u)$ **cancels identically** with $\frac{1 - u}{1 + u}$:
$$Q(u) = R(u) \frac{1 - u}{1 + u} = \frac{1 + 2u + u^2 + u^3}{1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3} = 1 + \frac{2 u^3}{1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q_k u^k.$$
Clearing the denominator $(1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3) Q(u) = 1 + 2u + u^2 + u^3$ gives an **integer** 3-term linear recurrence for $q_k$:
$$q_0 = 1, \quad q_1 = 0, \quad q_2 = 0, \quad q_3 = 2, \quad q_k = -2 q_{k-1} - q_{k-2} + q_{k-3} \quad (k \ge 4).$$
Finally, extracting $[u^n] \big(Q(u) (1 + u)^{2n}\big)$ gives the $O(n)$ closed-form sum:
$$[z^n] F(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} q_k \binom{2n}{n - k} \pmod{p}.$$

#### 3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 1, 2, 3, 4$)

Computing the first few terms of $q_k$:
$$q_0 = 1,\;\; q_1 = 0,\;\; q_2 = 0,\;\; q_3 = 2,\;\; q_4 = -2(2) - 0 + 0 = -4.$$
- **$n = 1$**: $q_0 \binom{2}{1} + q_1 \binom{2}{0} = 1 \cdot 2 + 0 = \mathbf{2}$.
- **$n = 2$**: $q_0 \binom{4}{2} + q_1 \binom{4}{1} + q_2 \binom{4}{0} = 1 \cdot 6 + 0 + 0 = \mathbf{6}$.
- **$n = 3$**: $q_0 \binom{6}{3} + q_3 \binom{6}{0} = 1 \cdot 20 + 2 \cdot 1 = \mathbf{22}$.
- **$n = 4$**: $q_0 \binom{8}{4} + q_3 \binom{8}{1} + q_4 \binom{8}{0} = 1 \cdot 70 + 2 \cdot 8 + (-4) \cdot 1 = 70 + 16 - 4 = \mathbf{82}$.
Every value matches the Stage 1 trace!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Failure Mode & Remedy: Using NTT or $\sqrt{1 - 4z}$ Newton Iteration Modulo an Arbitrary Prime $p$

- **Failure Mode**: Attempting to compute $C(z) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4z}}{2z}$ and invert $(1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3)$ in the $z$-domain via polynomial `sqrt` and `inv` requires NTT, which fails or requires slow 3-prime MTT when $p \in [10^8, 10^9 + 9]$ is an arbitrary prime given at runtime.
- **Remedy**: Whenever an algebraic generating function is a rational function $R(u(z))$ of a generalized binomial/Catalan parameter $u = z(1 + u)^t$, **never expand $u(z)$ in the $z$-domain**! Change variables to $u$ via the Formal Residue Theorem so that the square root disappears completely and $Q(u) = R(u)\frac{1 - (t-1)u}{1 + u}$ becomes a fixed low-degree rational function unrolled in $O(n)$ integer operations.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm Contract: Formal Residue Catalan Extraction (`CF 1930I`)

- **Input**: Integer $n \le 5 \times 10^5$ and arbitrary prime $p > 2n$.
- **Preconditions**: Arbitrary prime $p > 2n$; binomial coefficients $\binom{2n}{n-k} \bmod p$ precomputed.
- **Output**: $[z^n] F(z) \bmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space (or $O(1)$ auxiliary space by updating $\binom{2n}{n-k}$ iteratively via $\binom{2n}{n-k} = \binom{2n}{n-k+1} \frac{n-k+1}{n+k}$).
- **Core Invariant**: At step $k$, $q_k = [u^k] \frac{1 + 2u + u^2 + u^3}{1 + 2u + u^2 - u^3} \bmod p$ and $C_{2n, n-k} = \binom{2n}{n-k} \bmod p$.
:::

```cpp
vector<long long> q(n + 1, 0);
q[0] = 1;
if (n >= 3) q[3] = 2;
for (int k = 4; k <= n; ++k) {
    q[k] = (-2 * q[k - 1] - q[k - 2] + q[k - 3]) % p;
    if (q[k] < 0) q[k] += p;
}
long long ans = 0;
for (int k = 0; k <= n; ++k) {
    ans = (ans + q[k] * C(2 * n, n - k, p)) % p;
}
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Complete Solution — CP-III.4 (#160: Luogu P4747 — Simple Permutations)</summary>

#### 1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad & The Albert–Atkinson–Klazar Decomposition

We want to count simple permutations $s_k$ of length $k$ for all $4 \le k \le n$ modulo $998244353$.

1. **Inflation Grammar of All Permutations**:
   Let $F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k!\, x^k = x + 2x^2 + 6x^3 + 24x^4 + 120x^5 + \dots$ be the ordinary generating function of all non-empty permutations, and let $S(y) = \sum_{k=4}^{\infty} s_k y^k$ be the OGF of simple permutations of length $\ge 4$.
   By the **Modular Decomposition (`析合树`) Theorem** (Albert & Atkinson 2005), every non-empty permutation $\pi$ falls into **exactly one** of four disjoint structural classes:
   - **Class 1 (Singleton)**: $\pi = [1]$ of length $1$, with OGF $x$.
   - **Class 2 (Ascending Join / `升序合点`)**: $\pi$ is obtained by inflating the identity permutation $[1, 2, \dots, m]$ ($m \ge 2$) with $m$ non-empty blocks $B_1, \dots, B_m$, where **no $B_i$ is itself an ascending join** (so the decomposition into $m$ ascending components is maximal and unique).
     Let $F_{\text{asc}}(x)$ be the OGF of ascending joins. Then a block that is not an ascending join has OGF $F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)$, so:
     $$F_{\text{asc}}(x) = \sum_{m=2}^{\infty} \big(F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)\big)^m = \frac{\big(F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)\big)^2}{1 - \big(F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)\big)}.$$
     Adding $F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)$ to both sides gives $F(x) = \frac{F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x)}{1 - (F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x))}$, which solves immediately to $F(x) - F_{\text{asc}}(x) = \frac{F(x)}{1 + F(x)}$, and therefore:
     $$F_{\text{asc}}(x) = F(x) - \frac{F(x)}{1 + F(x)} = \frac{F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)}.$$
   - **Class 3 (Descending Join / `降序合点`)**: By reversal symmetry, descending joins of $m \ge 2$ non-descending blocks have the exact same OGF:
     $$F_{\text{desc}}(x) = \frac{F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)}.$$
   - **Class 4 (Simple Root / `析点`)**: $\pi$ is obtained by inflating a unique simple permutation $\sigma$ of length $m \ge 4$ with $m$ **arbitrary** non-empty permutations $B_1, \dots, B_m$. Summing over $m \ge 4$ gives the composition:
     $$\sum_{m=4}^{\infty} s_m \, F(x)^m = S\big(F(x)\big).$$

2. **Isolating $S(y)$ via Compositional Inversion (`Ch 10 §10.2–10.3`)**:
   Summing the four disjoint classes yields the fundamental implicit functional equation:
   $$F(x) = x + \frac{2 F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)} + S\big(F(x)\big).$$
   Notice that $F(x) = x + 2x^2 + \dots$ has valuation $1$ and $[x^1]F(x) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times$, so $F(x)$ possesses a unique compositional inverse $G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y) \in y \mathbb{F}_p[[y]]$ satisfying $F(G(y)) = y$.
   Substituting $x = G(y)$ (so $F(x) = y$) into the functional equation isolates $S(y)$ directly:
   $$y = G(y) + \frac{2y^2}{1 + y} + S(y) \implies S(y) = \frac{y(1 - y)}{1 + y} - G(y).$$
   Expanding $\frac{y(1 - y)}{1 + y} = y - 2y^2 + 2y^3 - 2y^4 + 2y^5 - \dots = y + 2\sum_{k=2}^{\infty} (-1)^{k-1} y^k$, we obtain for every $k \ge 4$:
   $$s_k = [y^k] S(y) = 2(-1)^{k-1} - [y^k] G(y).$$

#### 2. Computing $G(y) = F^{\langle -1 \rangle}(y)$ via Implicit Newton Iteration (`Ch 10`)

To find $G(y) \bmod y^{n+1}$ using strictly Part III (`<= Ch 13`) tools, we apply **Newton Iteration** (`Ch 10 §10.2`) to the implicit equation:
$$H(G) := F\big(G(y)\big) - y = 0.$$
Suppose we know $G_d(y) \equiv G(y) \pmod{y^d}$ (starting with $G_2(y) = y \bmod y^2$). Then one Newton step doubles the precision to $y^{2d}$:
$$G_{2d}(y) = G_d(y) - \frac{F\big(G_d(y)\big) - y}{F'\big(G_d(y)\big)} \bmod y^{2d}.$$
*(Alternative `Ch 09` CDQ / Relaxed Convolution Route)*: We can also write $F(x) = x + \frac{2F^2}{1+F} + S(F)$ as $S(F(x)) = F(x)\frac{1 - F(x)}{1 + F(x)} - x$, or compute the coefficients of $G(y)$ via semi-online CDQ / Newton composition in $O(n \log^2 n)$ time.

#### 3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace ($k = 4, 5$)

Let us invert $F(x) = x + 2x^2 + 6x^3 + 24x^4 + 120x^5 + O(x^6)$ by hand up to $y^5$:
- Set $G(y) = y + g_2 y^2 + g_3 y^3 + g_4 y^4 + g_5 y^5 + O(y^6)$.
- $[y^2] F(G(y)) = g_2 + 2 = 0 \implies g_2 = -2$.
- $[y^3] F(G(y)) = g_3 + 2(2 g_2) + 6 = g_3 - 8 + 6 = 0 \implies g_3 = 2$.
- $[y^4] F(G(y)) = g_4 + 2(2 g_3 + g_2^2) + 6(3 g_2) + 24 = g_4 + 16 - 36 + 24 = 0 \implies g_4 = -4$.
- $[y^5] F(G(y)) = g_5 + 2(2 g_4 + 2 g_2 g_3) + 6(3 g_3 + 3 g_2^2) + 24(4 g_2) + 120 = g_5 - 32 + 108 - 192 + 120 = 0 \implies g_5 = -4$.
- Substituting into $s_k = 2(-1)^{k-1} - g_k$:
  - $s_2 = -2 - (-2) = 0$.
  - $s_3 = 2 - 2 = 0$.
  - $s_4 = -2 - (-4) = \mathbf{2}$.
  - $s_5 = 2 - (-4) = \mathbf{6}$.
  All values match Stage 1!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Failure Mode & Remedy: Double-Counting Monotone Joins of Length $\ge 3$

- **Failure Mode**: Writing the inflation of ascending joins as $\sum_{m \ge 2} F(x)^m = \frac{F(x)^2}{1 - F(x)}$ instead of $\sum_{m \ge 2} \left(\frac{F(x)}{1 + F(x)}\right)^m = \frac{F(x)^2}{1 + F(x)}$ massively overcounts every ascending join of length $m \ge 3$ (for instance, $[1, 2, 3]$ would be counted as $[1, 2]$ inflated by $([1], [1, 2])$, as $[1, 2]$ inflated by $([1, 2], [1])$, and as $[1, 2, 3]$ inflated by $([1], [1], [1])$).
- **Remedy**: In any associative join operation (like ascending joins or series/parallel networks in `Ch 12`), the children of an ascending node **must not** be ascending nodes themselves (`F_non_asc = F - F_asc = F / (1 + F)`). Always enforce canonical alternation between node types!
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm Contract: Simple Permutation Enumeration (`Luogu P4747`)

- **Input**: Integer $n \in [4, 10^5]$.
- **Preconditions**: $F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n k!\,x^k$ has $[x^0]F(x) = 0$ and $[x^1]F(x) = 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{998244353}$.
- **Output**: Sequence $s_4, s_5, \dots, s_n \bmod 998244353$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ (or $O(n \log^2 n)$ with divide-and-conquer polynomial composition inside Newton's step) and $O(n)$ space.
- **Core Invariant**: After each doubling step $d \to 2d$, $F(G_{2d}(y)) \equiv y \pmod{y^{2d}}$, and $s_k = \big(2(-1)^{k-1} - [y^k]G(y)\big) \bmod 998244353$ for all $4 \le k \le n$.
:::

<details>
<summary>Complete Solution — CP-III.5 (#119: Codeforces 1528F — AmShZ Farm)</summary>

#### 1. Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad: Pollak's Circular Orbit & Raney's Lemma

We need to compute $\sum_{a \text{ valid}} \sum_{v=1}^{n} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k \pmod{998244353}$ for $n \le 10^9$ and $k \le 10^5$.

1. **Why Direct Enumeration Fails & The Diagnostic Signal**:
   The number of valid parking sequences is $(n + 1)^{n - 1}$, and $n \le 10^9$ is far too large for an $O(n)$ DP. The diagnostic signal for **Raney's Cycle Lemma / Pollak's Circle Argument (`Ch 11 §11.3`)** is the prefix-dominance condition $\lvert \{j : a_j \le i\} \rvert \ge i$ for $i = 1 \dots n$: if we let $c_v = \operatorname{occ}(v, a)$ be the number of cars preferring spot $v$, then $\sum_{v=1}^{n} c_v = n$ and $\sum_{v=1}^{i} (c_v - 1) \ge 0$ for all $1 \le i \le n$.

2. **Closing the Street into a Circle of $n + 1$ Spaces**:
   Add a dummy parking space $n + 1$ and arrange spaces $1, 2, \dots, n + 1$ clockwise around a circle. Now consider the set $\mathcal{U} = \{1, 2, \dots, n + 1\}^n$ of all $(n + 1)^n$ unrestricted preference sequences.
   - When $n$ cars park on the circle of $n + 1$ spaces (wrapping around modulo $n + 1$), all $n$ cars park and **exactly one space remains empty**.
   - Define the cyclic shift $\sigma(a) = \big((a_1 \bmod (n+1)) + 1, \dots, (a_n \bmod (n+1)) + 1\big)$. Shifting every car's preference by $+1 \bmod (n + 1)$ simply rotates the entire parking process by $+1 \bmod (n + 1)$, so the unique empty space also rotates by $+1 \bmod (n + 1)$!
   - Since $\gcd(n, n + 1) = 1$, every orbit $\{a, \sigma(a), \dots, \sigma^n(a)\}$ has size $n + 1$, and **exactly one** sequence $a^*$ in each orbit leaves space $n + 1$ empty!
   - A sequence leaves space $n + 1$ empty without wrapping around if and only if $a^* \in \{1, \dots, n\}^n$ is a valid parking sequence! Moreover, because $a^* \in \{1, \dots, n\}^n$, we have:
     $$\operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a^*) = 0 \implies \sum_{v=1}^{n} \operatorname{occ}(v, a^*)^k = \sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a^*)^k.$$
   - Crucially, the cyclic shift $\sigma$ simply permutes the labels $1, 2, \dots, n + 1$, so the sum $\sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k$ is **constant across all $n + 1$ members of each orbit**!

#### 2. Binomial-Moment Collapse via Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind (`Ch 06 §6.4`)

Averaging over the $n + 1$ shifts in every orbit reduces the constrained sum over valid parking sequences to an **unconstrained** sum over all $(n + 1)^n$ sequences in $\{1, \dots, n + 1\}^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans} &= \frac{1}{n + 1} \sum_{a \in \{1, \dots, n+1\}^n} \sum_{v=1}^{n+1} \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k \\
&= \frac{1}{n + 1} \cdot (n + 1) \sum_{a \in \{1, \dots, n+1\}^n} \operatorname{occ}(1, a)^k \\
&= \sum_{m=1}^{n} \binom{n}{m} n^{n - m} \, m^k.
\end{aligned}$$
Here $\binom{n}{m} n^{n - m}$ counts the sequences $a \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\}^n$ in which spot $1$ appears $m$ times and the remaining $n - m$ positions are chosen from $\{2, \dots, n + 1\}$.

To evaluate $\sum_{m=1}^{n} \binom{n}{m} n^{n - m} m^k$ in $O(k \log k)$ time when $n \le 10^9$ and $k \le 10^5$, expand $m^k$ in the falling-factorial basis using Stirling numbers of the second kind (`Ch 06 §6.4`):
$$m^k = \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} m^{\underline{j}}.$$
Using the absorption identity $\binom{n}{m} m^{\underline{j}} = n^{\underline{j}} \binom{n - j}{m - j}$ and swapping the sums gives:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Ans} &= \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} n^{\underline{j}} \sum_{m=j}^{n} \binom{n - j}{m - j} n^{(n - j) - (m - j)} \\
&= \sum_{j=1}^{\min(n, k)} \left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} n^{\underline{j}} \, (n + 1)^{n - j} \pmod{998244353}.
\end{aligned}$$
Finally, the $k$-th row of Stirling numbers $\left\{\begin{matrix} k \\ j \end{matrix}\right\} = \sum_{i=0}^{j} \frac{(-1)^{j - i}}{(j - i)!} \frac{i^k}{i!}$ is computed in a single NTT convolution of length $2k$ in $O(k \log k)$ time.

#### 3. Verification on the Hand-Checkable Trace ($n = 2, 3;\; k = 2$)

For $k = 2$, $\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1$ and $\left\{\begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right\} = 1$:
- **$n = 2, k = 2$**: $1 \cdot 2^{\underline{1}} \cdot 3^{2 - 1} + 1 \cdot 2^{\underline{2}} \cdot 3^{2 - 2} = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6 + 2 = \mathbf{8}$.
- **$n = 3, k = 2$**: $1 \cdot 3^{\underline{1}} \cdot 4^{3 - 1} + 1 \cdot 3^{\underline{2}} \cdot 4^{3 - 2} = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 16 + 1 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 = 48 + 24 = \mathbf{72}$.
Both match Stage 1!

::: {.callout-warning}
## Failure Mode & Remedy: Negative Exponents $n - j < 0$ or $0^k$ at $v = n + 1$

- **Failure Mode**:
  1. When $n < k$, summing $j$ up to $k$ instead of $\min(n, k)$ attempts to evaluate $(n + 1)^{n - j}$ for $n - j < 0$ even though $n^{\underline{j}} = 0$ for all $j > n$.
  2. If $k = 0$ were ever queried, $\operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a^*)^0 = 0^0 = 1 \neq 0$, so spot $n + 1$ would contribute $+1$ to the orbit sum and require subtracting $(n + 1)^{n - 1}$. Because $k \ge 1$, $0^k = 0$, so $\operatorname{occ}(n + 1, a^*)^k = 0$ holds cleanly.
- **Remedy**: Always clamp the upper summation limit to $J = \min(n, k)$ and maintain $n^{\underline{j}} \bmod p$ and $(n + 1)^{n - j} \bmod p$ iteratively for $1 \le j \le J$.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Algorithm Contract: Parking Sequence Frequency Moments (`CF 1528F`)

- **Input**: Integers $n \in [1, 10^9]$ and $k \in [1, 10^5]$.
- **Preconditions**: Modulus $p = 998244353 > k$.
- **Output**: $\sum_{a \text{ valid}} \sum_{v=1}^n \operatorname{occ}(v, a)^k \bmod 998244353$.
- **Complexity**: $O(k \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ space.
- **Core Invariant**: After the NTT convolution $S = A * B$ with $A_i = i^k / i!$ and $B_i = (-1)^i / i!$, $S_j = \left\{\begin{smallmatrix} k \\ j \end{smallmatrix}\right\} \bmod p$ for all $0 \le j \le k$.
:::

```cpp
// Compute Stirling S2 row k via single NTT convolution:
Poly A(k + 1), B(k + 1);
for (int i = 0; i <= k; ++i) {
    A[i] = qpow(i, k) * inv_fact[i] % MOD;
    B[i] = (i & 1 ? MOD - inv_fact[i] : inv_fact[i]);
}
Poly S = multiply(A, B); // S[j] = {k \brace j}
long long ans = 0, fall_n = 1;
int lim = min<long long>(n, k);
long long pw = qpow((n + 1) % MOD, n - 1), inv_n1 = qpow((n + 1) % MOD, MOD - 2);
for (int j = 1; j <= lim; ++j) {
    fall_n = fall_n * ((n - j + 1) % MOD) % MOD;
    ans = (ans + S[j] * fall_n % MOD * pw) % MOD;
    pw = pw * inv_n1 % MOD;
}
```

</details>
